items.title: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks - NBC News
items.summary: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks  NBC News
items.content:
Ukrainians take shelter in Holosiivska metro station during an overnight Russian attack on Kyiv, in August. Danylo Antoniuk / Future Publishing via Getty
Nov. 2, 2026, 5:14 AM EST  /  Updated   Nov. 2, 2026, 7:56 AM EST
Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.
Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace.
Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out.
A translated screenshot of alerts sent by hackers to Ukraine's emergency alert application. Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communication / via X
The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights.
Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile.
That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts.
Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s “Air Alert” app had likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm.
In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. It later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said.
Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal.
“I was outside with my dog when the first alert came,” said Olena Yermakova, 32, a researcher in Kyiv.
She picked up her dog and ran inside, she said, before checking the news to see what was happening.
Because the message was in Russian, “I thought it was a hack by the Russians,” she said. “But the seconds before that were absolutely terrifying. I started running through a checklist in my head of what to do during a nuclear threat and whether I had all the supplies at home, and my hands started shaking.”
Still, many other Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake, and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” one user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.”
The state emergency service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the “Air Alert” app.
Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application has suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.”
Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official.
Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.
It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson.
The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the frontline town of Oleshky , which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.
Buses carrying evacuees from the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky arrive in the Chernihiv region on Saturday. Diego Fedele/Getty; Efrem Lukatsky/AP
The truce amounted to the biggest de-escalation between Kyiv and Moscow since the war started in early 2022.
“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” Melania Trump said in a post on X on Sunday. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”
Ukraine’s ombudsman ​for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said he was exploring opportunities for “further humanitarian initiatives” with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, adding that it was “important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation.”
Before the truce took hold, the United Nations estimated that some 2,000 civilians remained in Oleshky, many experiencing hunger and unable to leave safely because of heavily mined roads.
Neither side has disclosed the exact number of people evacuated, but the first lady said Sunday it was nearly 800. The evacuees could go into territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the town, officials on both sides said.
Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, said Monday that she had expected more people to evacuate from Oleshky, saying “quite a few empty buses” left the area. Many people chose to stay because they couldn’t leave elderly or sick loved ones, she said, or simply refused to leave their homes no matter what.
She said for those remaining, humanitarian aid deliveries would take place at least monthly, with the “coordination and mediation” of Melania Trump.
Ukraine’s armed forces accused Russia on Monday of using the truce to rotate its units and fortify positions in the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Kyiv also could have used the ceasefire to regroup, calling it a “completely common practice in such situations.”

items.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
items.summary: The airline says fuel prices may rise by €2bn in 2028 unless there is an end to the US-Israel war with Iran.
items.content:
By Mitchell Labiak ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Theo Leggett ,Â  Business correspondent
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be â¬2bn (Â£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to â¬2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" â in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices â the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

items.title: ‘Sharper, longer slowdown’ predicted for Australian economy as fifth interest rate hike looms
items.summary: Australia’s central bank expected to hit mortgage holders again on Tuesday, as war in Middle East combines with collapsing house pricesGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastAustralia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, majo
items.content:
The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, pushing the cash rate to its highest since 2008. Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty Images
The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, pushing the cash rate to its highest since 2008. Photograph: Andrew Merry/Getty Images
‘Sharper, longer slowdown’ predicted for Australian economy as fifth interest rate hike looms
Australia’s central bank expected to hit mortgage holders again on Tuesday, as war in Middle East combines with collapsing house prices
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures.
The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession.
The RBA may be about to hike interest rates. Use our loan calculator to check how it may affect you
Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%.
Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections.
Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”.
Sharper, longer slowdown graph. This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said.
“Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.”
Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared.
Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook , analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts.
Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials.
The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year.
The RBA has primed the market for an interest rate rise. But what will it mean for unemployment? | Greg Jericho
Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation.
The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe.
Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved.
As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again.
Historically large graph. The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record.
Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak.
Drawing from RBA research, Oliver said a property correction of that magnitude could deliver a substantial hit to the economy, as worried homeowners pull back on spending – a phenomenon known as the “wealth effect”.
A weakening property market will also weigh on homebuilding, Oliver said, adding to the multiplying pressures on the economy.
While an economic contraction was not his “base case”, he warned there was a “significant and rising” risk of recession, the chance of which would rise to as high as 45% should the RBA hike as expected on Tuesday.

items.title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war - The Guardian
items.summary: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war  The Guardian
items.content:
The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year. Photograph: Reuters
The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year. Photograph: Reuters
Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

items.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
items.summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
items.content:
Figure caption, 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Image source, TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images
Image caption, Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
Image caption, An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

items.title: Israel hopes third Iran war will differ from Gaza conflict with Hamas - The Jerusalem Post
items.summary: Israel hopes third Iran war will differ from Gaza conflict with Hamas  The Jerusalem Post
items.content:
How Israel hopes third war with Iran will be different than Gaza - analysis
Some top officials hope unique advantages held over Iran will avoid the repeat of endless “rounds” similar to what Israel has had with Hamas.
Smoke and flames rise at the site of airstrikes on an oil depot in Tehran on March 7, 2026.
( photo credit : Sasan / Middle East Images / AFP via Getty Images )
Many Israelis expect a third round of war between the US-Israel and Iran – and whoever else in the region Tehran pulls in. The next question many have is: Will this really be the last battle or just another “round” in a series of new, seemingly endless rounds?
Israelis’ experience with seemingly endless rounds of fighting can be seen on multiple fronts.
But it is most fresh regarding Gaza , where major conflicts were fought in 2008-9, 2012, 2014, 2021, along with another half-dozen or so minor conflicts, all before October 7.
If so, might Iran just become the new Gaza problem?
In other words, might Iran become an adversary who is too scary to go all out against and so cannot be completely beaten but only contained, deterred, and delayed from perpetrating future attacks on Israel?
Palestinians walk past a destroyed Israeli armored vehicle left behind by the Israeli army during the recent war, in the Tel al-Hawa neighborhood of Gaza City, September 7, 2026. (credit: ABED RAHIM KHATIB/FLASH90)
Might Iran become an unending series of “hiccups” when ballistic missiles rain down on all of Israel’s cities (not, like old days with Hamas, “just Sderot”), and the whole country shuts down with people hiding in their bomb shelters?
What will that mean for routine life, foreign investment, and the constant need to produce hugely expensive air-defense interceptors, not to mention air travel?
This is assuming that Israel maintains the heavy upper hand and the Islamic Republic does not, at some point, surprise Jerusalem with a new weapon or tactic which could cause far more harm.
With all of those questions, why would Israel roll the dice to attack now, when there is no immediate danger from Iran either with respect to its nuclear or ballistic missile program? Both those issues could eventually return to being threats, but they are not expected to be major or imminent for several years.
There are at least two hopeful factors which some Israeli officials think could make this third round more effective – and the general struggle against Iran more successful and faster than the drawn-out, almost 20-year struggle with Hamas .
Officials point out that there are tens of millions of Iranians who hate the regime and want to tear it down – a much more formidable challenge for internal rebellion than Hamas ever faced in Gaza.
They also point out that Israel has the most powerful country in the world – the United States – fighting side-by-side, or in this case fighter jet squadron-by-squadron.
There are numerous counterpoints which could make Iran’s regime harder to topple than Hamas, not least that a major land operation is either politically impossible or militarily highly impractical.
When Hamas said it could wait out Israel during another round, it had almost zero opposition, and it was saying it could wait out a small country of 10 million people whose economy is highly vulnerable to minor disruptions.
By contrast, a million Iranians came out to protest against Iran’s regime on January 8-9, and the American military has maintained a show of force and economic pressure now for most of 2026 in a way that Israel could never have done.
Even Israel’s October 7 war with Hamas was never really two years long. It was usually a few weeks of intense fighting, followed by months of much lower-key patrolling or even withdrawing until another fight.
Optimistic to believe Tehran may bend on nuclear issue
So optimistic Israeli officials think that the regime in Tehran may really either bend on the nuclear issue or even be toppled at some point by an additional round of attacks combined with pressure.
After dropping more than 30,000 bombs on Iran over 40 days in early 2026 did not achieve nuclear concessions, let alone topple the regime, they would be blind to assume victory is around the corner.
But that does not mean that their gamble – if it happens – might not pay off.
Whether it will be worth the cost to the Israeli home front will be a much more complex calculation.

Share How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge on social media
ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits from almost $10bn to more than $15bn [File: Dado Ruvic/Reuters]
United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections .
The estimate, released by The New York Times, is a conservative evaluation based on the performance of 51 large US oil and gas companies in the six months from April through September. By contrast, in the same period in 2025 – when the prices of oil were lower prior to the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran – they collectively earned less than $47bn.

But the gains come as burgeoning living costs are crushing consumers. Americans have spent an extra $150bn on petrol and diesel since the war on Iran began on February 28, according to an analysis by Brown University ’s Climate Solutions Lab, which amounts to more than $1,150 per household.
The disparity has fuelled a political debate over who gains and who pays the price for the war. Responding to Trump, Democratic Representative Jim McGovern wrote on X: “We’re not making a ‘freaking fortune,’ we’re PAYING a ‘freaking fortune’.”
Naser al-Tamimi, a fellow at the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI) in Milan, Italy, said US energy companies have benefitted from the war in different ways. “Crude producers gain from higher oil prices, while refiners capture exceptional margins as diesel and other fuel supplies tighten,” he said.
Additionally, “damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refineries, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipments , and sanctions-related trade frictions have intensified shortages”, while “relatively secure US facilities and access to discounted crude strengthen these gains”.
ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits of between $10bn and $15bn. While the gains are considerable, The New York Times found they generally remained below 2022 levels, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused oil prices to soar to roughly $100 a barrel and raised natural gas prices, compared with the current average of $90 from April through September.
American refining companies also reaped greater profits as global fuel supplies tightened and inventories depleted due to heavy damage to infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia. Valero Energy’s third-quarter profit increased more than sixfold, reaching $6.83bn. Phillips 66 announced its highest quarterly profit on record, with net income jumping to $5.62bn from $133m a year earlier.
Geoffrey Miller, geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, said the US-Israel war with Iran “created the largest supply-side shock to global oil and refined products markets in years”.
Miller added that the war “created a risk premium that US-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise”. By contrast, Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult”.
Tehran retaliated against the US-Israeli attack by launching missiles and drones at the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, found Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six GCC member states. Despite claims by Iranian officials that they were targeting US military facilities, they also hit energy infrastructure.
Iran also effectively blocked passage of most vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil and gas – the tit-for-tat steps raising the risks of transporting energy out of the crucial passageway.
Analysts warned of continued volatility until a durable political settlement between the US and Iran is reached. Oil prices dropped briefly in the summer after a memorandum of understanding was signed in June, but prices quickly soared again when talks broke down.
A more recent escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has further compounded the crisis: the Bab al-Mandeb strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which Saudi Arabia uses to export oil, is now also a theatre of war.
“In the short term, windfall profits will only strengthen oil company balance sheets and shareholder returns,” Miller said. “However, the big profits come with a major caveat. That’s because over the longer term, high oil prices risk harming economic growth prospects and could even contribute towards the outbreak of a recession, which would in turn be likely to lead to reduced demand for oil” and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank’s global economics and markets team in London, said it was likely that the prices of key energy products would remain high given the uncertainty about the duration of the war in Iran.
“Prices in all markets that have an exposure to this global supply shock – which includes the US – will face high prices also next year, and consumers will continue to feel this price pressure unless governments step in,” Schmit told Al Jazeera.
The US-led war on Iran has raised costs for oil, transport fuels, gas, electricity and food. According to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, commodity prices are set to rise 23 percent this year, as disrupted grain shipments and the El Nino weather phenomenon also threaten harvests and food affordability.
The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization said on October 2 that world food commodity prices rose a further 1.5 percent in September, after reaching their highest level since late 2022 in August, amid adverse weather and trade disruptions in the Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has sought to blame high global fuel prices on Ukraine and pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries, even as Moscow continued to wage attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The US president has argued that a deal with Russia reversing years of sanctions would help lower diesel prices.
In the Gulf, analysts said higher oil prices will benefit exporters that can maintain shipments, but prolonged insecurity will continue to threaten supply reliability and investment.
“Gulf producers face years of reconstruction and pressure to diversify export routes,” ISPI’s al-Tamimi said. “A diplomatic settlement could ease prices, whereas renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran risk triggering another regional war, further disrupting Hormuz and prolonging shortages.”

items.content:
US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Apple Earnings as Binance Hack, Oil Prices and Midterm Elections Take Focus: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street bull ©Shutterstock US stock futures moved higher on Monday, pointing to a potential recovery on Wall Street following October's technology-led selloff, as investors prepared for major corporate earnings, the US midterm elections and further developments in the Middle East.
Apple's upcoming financial results are attracting particular attention, with new Chief Executive John Ternus preparing to lead his first earnings conference call. Meanwhile, a reported multibillion-dollar security breach at cryptocurrency exchange Binance has raised concerns about digital asset security.
Oil prices also declined sharply as investors assessed the possibility of diplomatic progress in the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
Apple Earnings to Test Growth Outlook Under New CEO
Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) is scheduled to report earnings on Monday, with investors focusing on the company's growth prospects, artificial intelligence strategy and the potential impact of higher component costs.
John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook as chief executive in September, will host his first earnings conference call in the role.
His appointment followed the introduction of several products, including Apple's first foldable iPhone, a smart home hub and its first touchscreen laptops. Shipments of these devices began during the company's current fiscal first quarter.
Investors will examine Apple's guidance for the important holiday shopping period, alongside management's plans for artificial intelligence and the updated Siri platform.
Rising memory chip prices are another area of concern, with analysts expecting higher production costs to affect profitability. Profit growth could slow to its weakest pace in six quarters.
Apple also regained its position as the world's most valuable publicly traded company on Friday, overtaking Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
Despite a 1.2% decline in Apple's share price, its market capitalisation stood at $5.03 trillion at the close. Nvidia's valuation fell to $4.93 trillion after its shares dropped 4.2%.
The shift came as investors reassessed the scale of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending and the time required for those investments to generate returns.
Binance Faces $3.64 Billion in Withdrawals Following Reported Hack
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance experienced customer withdrawals totalling $3.64 billion after resuming operations following a major security breach reportedly linked to North Korea.
The withdrawals represented approximately 2.1% of the platform's assets.
The incident reportedly involved the theft of $6.3 billion from the exchange during the previous week, raising questions about security and confidence across the cryptocurrency industry.
Binance said withdrawal activity was stabilising following an initial surge and reported that customer deposits remained substantial.
As of 28 October, the exchange reported total assets under management of $171 billion and approximately 335 million registered users worldwide.
Cryptocurrency prices showed signs of stabilisation following recent losses.
Bitcoin (COIN:BTCUSD) recovered above $78,000 on Monday after reaching a six-week low on Friday.
Ether (COIN:ETHUSD) also rebounded modestly to approximately $2,287, following a decline to its lowest level in two months.
Market participants remain attentive to customer flows and the potential consequences of the reported breach for confidence in digital asset platforms.
Wall Street Futures Advance Following October Technology Selloff
US stock index futures rose in early Monday trading, suggesting a stronger opening following the previous month's weakness in technology shares.
By 03:50 ET, S&P 500 futures had gained 0.46% to 7,614 points, while Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 0.75% to 28,753 points. Dow Jones futures increased 0.28% to 52,075 points.
Technology stocks also recovered across Asian markets, helping support sentiment towards US equity futures.
Investors are preparing for another active earnings week, with Apple due to publish results on Monday and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) scheduled to report on Tuesday.
Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Berkshire Hathaway are also expected to release financial results on Monday.
The announcements will provide further information about corporate profitability, technology spending and the outlook for major US businesses.
Oil Prices Fall More Than 3% Amid Renewed Diplomatic Expectations
Crude oil prices declined sharply on Monday as investors assessed prospects for diplomatic progress in the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
Brent crude futures for January delivery fell 3.3% to $109.70 per barrel by 00:27 ET, while US West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 3.5% to $100.48 per barrel.
The decline followed a strong October rally, during which both benchmarks gained nearly 15%.
The absence of a major escalation over the weekend encouraged some traders to take profits after recent price increases.
According to a report by Axios, President Donald Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a Saturday telephone conversation that he preferred to allow more time for diplomacy before deciding whether to resume military operations.
The report also indicated that Netanyahu favoured renewed US strikes shortly after the midterm elections.
Lower crude prices could help reduce energy-related inflation pressures for businesses and consumers.
However, oil prices remain elevated following October's gains, leaving markets sensitive to further developments in the conflict and potential supply disruptions.
US Midterm Elections Bring Fiscal and Regulatory Policy Into Focus
The US midterm elections scheduled for Tuesday represent another important event for financial markets, with the results set to determine the composition of Congress during the second half of President Donald Trump's term.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are being contested.
The elections take place against a backdrop of concerns about elevated gasoline prices and the prolonged conflict with Iran.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey placed Trump's approval rating at 31%, the lowest level recorded in that poll.
The composition of the next Congress could influence the administration's ability to advance legislation covering fiscal policy, trade, taxation and regulation.
If Democrats secure control of both chambers, the administration could face greater legislative obstacles. A divided Congress could also increase reliance on executive actions in areas where legislation proves difficult.
For investors, the election results may affect expectations for government spending, business regulation and the broader economic policy environment.
Wall Street enters the new trading week with several important developments influencing investor sentiment.
Apple's earnings and other major corporate results will provide fresh evidence about technology demand, profitability and artificial intelligence investment.
At the same time, the reported Binance security breach has increased scrutiny of cryptocurrency markets, while declining oil prices have offered some relief from inflation concerns.
The US midterm elections and developments in the Iran conflict remain additional sources of uncertainty, with potential implications for fiscal policy, energy markets and broader financial conditions.

San Mateo to expand Delaware basin gas processing capacity under new producer agreements
The project adds about $25 million to San Mateo’s 2026 midstream capital budget, bringing it to $170-190 million, while total processing capacity is expected to exceed 1.3 bcfd.
Assets owned and operated by Matador Resources and its midstream joint venture, San Mateo, include over 1000 miles of pipelines, 20 saltwater disposal wells and processing plants with over 1 bcfd of natural gas processing capacity.
San Mateo Midstream LLC plans to expand natural gas gathering and processing infrastructure in New Mexico's Delaware basin after signing two long-term agreements with a producer.
Matador Resources, Five Point Capital form Delaware basin midstream JV
San Mateo Midstream, a joint venture of Matador Resources Co. (51%) and Five Point Infrastructure LLC (49%), said the agreements are expected to add long-term volumes across its gathering and processing system. With that and anticipated production growth from Matador, the company plans to expand its Marlan natural gas processing complex in Eddy County, NM, with a 300-MMcfd processing train and a new nitrogen rejection unit. The company also expects to construct about 20 miles of natural gas pipeline to connect newly dedicated acreage and a field treating facility for CO 2 removal.
Subject to permitting, procurement, and construction activities, the Marlan expansion is targeted for completion by yearend 2028.
The company said the project will increase its expected 2026 midstream capital expenditures by about $25 million, raising its estimated midstream capital budget for the year to $170-190 million.
The agreements consist of a new long-term fixed-fee gas gathering and processing contract and an extension of an existing gas gathering and processing agreement.
Under the new agreement, San Mateo will gather and treat natural gas from newly dedicated acreage in Lea and Eddy Counties, NM, and process the volumes at the Marlan complex. The agreement includes a large-scale acreage dedication in the northern Delaware basin.
Separately, San Mateo amended an existing gas gathering and processing agreement covering production from Eddy County. Under the extension, gas will continue to be gathered, treated, and processed at the Black River gas processing plant in Eddy County for several years beyond the original contract term. The extension builds on a gas gathering and processing agreement San Mateo announced in October 2018, the company noted.
Upon completion of the Marlan expansion, San Mateo's total natural gas processing capacity will exceed 1.3 bcfd, nearly tripling the 460-MMcfd capacity it had before Matador contributed Pronto Midstream LLC to the venture in December 2024.

Matador Resources Co. and San Mateo Midstream LLC completed and commissioned an expansion of San Mateo's Black River cryogenic natural gas processing plant in Eddy County, NM.
San Mateo wraps Delaware basin gas plant expansion, updates pipeline projects
Joseph Wm. Foran, Matador founder, chairman, and chief executive officer, and founder of San Mateo, said the agreements build on San Mateo's growth.
"Following the closing of the previously announced Cardinal Midstream acquisition in the third quarter, we completed the connection of the San Mateo and Cardinal systems in southern Eddy County, New Mexico," he said.
"In 2027, San Mateo plans to complete the full system connection with a northern pipeline connecting San Mateo's Lea County gathering infrastructure with the terminus of Cardinal's gathering infrastructure in Eddy County. This connection is expected to allow gas volumes to flow from the Marlan Plant complex in the north to the Pecos River Plant in the south, providing further flexibility for San Mateo and its customers."
He said the newly signed agreements are expected to increase volumes beginning in 2028.

Geopolitics & Retreating Oil: Over the weekend, President Trump told supporters that the U.S. will " put it away very soon " regarding the conflict with Iran, stating, "Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it." French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests
Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living.
The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.
As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end the lycée blockades , which have been running since September and have prompted one of the biggest protest movements and social crises of his presidency.
From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demanding more replacement teachers and repairs to buildings barricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.
Students gather outside a blockaded high school in Paris to protest against a lack of resources. Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/AP University students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities across France to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.
Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.
He said measures offered by the government last week to cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.
He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”
Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.
A protester adds a bin to a fire outside the Montebello international high school in Lille. Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty Images In Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.

He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.

items.content:
Stock market after midterm elections: S&P 500 history
The S&P 500 averaged a 13.7% one-year gain after 11 midterm elections since 1980.
After divided-government outcomes, the index averaged a 15% one-year gain, compared to 11.5% under single-party control.
Fed policy, earnings and the AI trade may matter more than the election result.
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.

items.title: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app - The Guardian
items.summary: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app  The Guardian
items.content:
Many residents of Kyiv ignored the alerts, which were sent at about 11pm on Sunday. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Many residents of Kyiv ignored the alerts, which were sent at about 11pm on Sunday. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
Residents in Kyiv also warned of chemical attack and street-to-street fighting in false message sent by unknown party
Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.
The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.
Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”
A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.
The false alerts on a smartphone. Photograph: AP In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.
One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.
The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.
Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.
There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.
Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.
Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.
The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region.
He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left.
Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said.
Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same.
Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

items.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
items.summary: The exchange froze transactions following the incident which has been linked to a North Korean group.
items.content:
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (Â£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack .
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with âthe fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.
"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.
AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

items.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
items.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
items.content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to make a deal.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state media.
The oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump is exercising his maximum optionality on Iran, says Richard Goldberg
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signalled they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
U.S.  West Texas Intermediate futures shed 7.4% to close at $96.46 a barrel, the biggest daily loss since July 27. Brent crude , the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to settle at $104.77 a barrel.
President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October.
The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again.
Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA.
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.
"With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said.

Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.
That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security.
UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations.
At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point.
However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach.
“Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
“Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.”
The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision.
That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said.
Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out.
The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged.
Byrne said a China strategy was an urgent concern as “Europe is changing fast” and “proposing new trade protections as it gets bolder with Beijing and warier of Washington”.
The new laws “may trap Britain outside EU trade walls, cutting us off from our largest market”.
Byrne said the government “should be prepared to consider dynamic alignment” with the EU include tariffs on EVs “as the price of securing British firms a place in the EU’s Made in Europe project” and to help guard against China dominance.
The UK is already under pressure to align with the EU on tariffs on EVs, but the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will make a decision in the best interests of the UK.
The EU has already imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, capped the number of hybrid cars that can be imported from China and is now considering a Franco-German proposal for a “kill switch” to block imports if China weaponises trade – as it did last year with curbs on exports of rare-earth minerals and chips. “The UK’s partners are moving further and faster,” the report noted.
China is now on track to surpass last year’s record $1.19tn trade surplus with the rest of the world.
Its latest five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, gives a glimpse of where China is going next in prioritising the strategic expansion of high-value green exports such as EVs, batteries, wind turbines, hydrogen and solar panels.
A government spokesperson said it did not accept the committee’s verdict. “We recognise the committee’s work on this report, but we disagree with its conclusion.”
They added that the government’s approach was “consistent” - it cooperated where it could and challenged where it must.
“Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise,” the spokesperson said.

"Rubio told reporters "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it."

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections.
On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.
Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.
On Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations."
In a Telegram post , the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."
Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.
The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

items.summary: Jos Leijdekkers has been found guilty in absentia of cocaine smuggling and is believed to be in Sierra Leone.
